MR. CHAIRMAN: Question No. 221.  
SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN: Mr. Chairman, Sir, a very serious situation is depicted by the 
hon. Minister's reply about our fertiliser consumption and fertiliser import. The agrarian crisis is 
deepening and dependence on urea import is increasing, reaching around 70 lakh tonnes in the 
current year, which is more than 35 per cent of the indgenous production of fertiliser. The import 
price is also continuously rising, now reaching 410 dollars per tonne, which is around Rs. 
16,000 per tonne, compared to the domestic cost of production of R£ 12,000 per tonne. In 
such a situation, my question to the hon. Minister is this. What is the share of the imported fertiliser 
in the total fertiliser subsidy bill of the Government? If it is a major part of the total subsdiy bill, 
how could the Government conceive of a policy of pr omoting investment in the urea sector 
based on international price parity benchmark, knowing the fact that import price is continuously 
increasing, now reaching a whopping 410 dollars per tonn? What is the logic of going into the 
international price parity policy ?

Coordination between States and Central Government on Agriculture  
t*222. SHRI RUDRA NARAYAN PANY: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state:  
(a)  how his Ministry co-ordinates with the Departments of Agriculture of the States; 
(b)  whether recently any conference of the Ministers of Agriculture of the States was 
convened in Delhi; 
(c)  the amount that would have been incurred on the genuine welfare of farmers in the 
country; so far; 
(d)  whether any conflict has arisen between the Central Government and the State 
Governments on the agriculture budget so far; and 
(e)  whether Government is contemplating to prepare 'Agriculture Budget' on the lines of 
'Railway Budgef? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a)to (e) A Statement 
is laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement  
(a) and (b) As Agriculture is a State subject, the States are responsible for implementation 
of policy and programmes for development of agriculture, and the Government of India 
supplements the efforts of the States through appropriate financial and policy support. The 
Ministry of Agriculture coordinates with the Departments of Agriculture of the States mainly 
through meetings and conferences of States, such as Kharif/Rabi Conference to obtain their 
views, suggestions and feedback on different programmes and policies of the Government 
for development of Agriculture; approval of Annual Work Plans of States after due 
consultation, and through the process of monitoring the implementation of different schemes 
sponsored by the Ministry. State Governments are also consulted on important policy 
measures. For example, while considering the recommendations .of National Commission 
on Farmers, States were consulted in a Conference of State Ministers of Agriculture and 
Allied Sectors on 23.12.2006.  
(c) The Plan Outlay of the three Departments under the Ministry of Agriculture during 
the last three years is as under:

2.     Deptt. of Animal Husbandry, Dairying & Fisheries      669 777 910  
3.     Deptt. of Agricultural Research & Education            1150 1350 1620

initiatives, including waiver of debt of farmers announced in the Budget 2008-09.

SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: To the first question which the hon. Member has asked, my reply

SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI: Mr. Chairman, thank you very much. I would like to know from 
the hon. Minister in connection with answers to question parts (b) & (e), where the reply is 'no'. 
My specific question is on the same issue. The hon. Minister, when he was in Maharashtra, 
made an announcement that the Government will consider increasing the limit of two hectares 
for waiver of debt. Therefore, I would like to know whether this was brought to the notice of the 
Agriculture Minister before the Budget was prepared, because the Minister is aware that, always, 
when the Finance Minister makes a statement here, he consults the Ministers in advance. I would 
like to know whether in this particular case, it was done or not; because, after the Budget, in 
Vidarbha region in Maharashtra, 34 farmers have committed suicide. I would like to know 
whether the Minister was aware that such things might happen and whether this proves that 
there is a difference of opinion between the hon. Prime Minister and the Finance Minister and 
also between the Finance Minister and the Agriculture Minister.  
On the same question, lastly, a number of times we have made a demand in the House that the 
Budget for farmers in the country should be an independent separate Budget as there is the 
Railway Budget. I would like to know whether the Minister agrees with this. Looking to his 
experience, I would like to know whether he would like to take steps in this regard.  

10    Oral Answers  [RAJYA SABHA]  to Questions  
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: The hon. former Speaker has put two questions. The first question 
is about differences among the hon. Prime Minister the Finance Minister and the Agriculture 
Minister. My reply is, there is no difference. What ever is the decision, it has been taken 
collectively.  
Regarding a separate Budget for agriculture, yes, this particular demand has been made on 
many occasions by many hon. Members; also, there are write-ups in some of the newspapers. 
We have to keep in mind that the agricultural sector has inter-sector linkages to water resources, 
irrigation, fertilizer, rural development, finance, cooperation, power, etc. There are separate 
Ministries for these issues. Hence, it is not possible to bring all these under one umbrella and one 
Ministry. That is why meeting the demand for a separate Budget for agriculture is not possible.  
DR. K. MALAISAMY: Sir, I would be brief as Mr. Chairman has directed. Sir, the role of 
Centre, as seen from the Minister's reply is to give financial and policy support to the States and it 
is okay. I am interested to know whether the total number of people who are involved in the 
agricultural operation in the country and the allocations given by the Centre are in proportion to 
each other? In other words, supposing 70 per cent are involved in agriculture, what is the total 
allocation they get out of the total Budget?  
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: In fact, one has to study the Budget but I have to just explain one 
thing that the total number of farmers in this country are somewhere near 12 crores. These are 
called in Hindi, Khatedars, i.e. who own the actual land. They are about 12 crores and if you see 
in the last two to three years, there is a consistent rise in Budgetary provision for agriculture 
from this Government.  
DR. K. MALAISAMY: My question is whether it is in proportion to the total agriculture.

Review of policy of permitting big retail corporates  
*223. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:ft 
SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA:  
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be 
pleased to state:  
Article I.  whether Government has lately reviewed its policy on permitting big retail 
corporates to expand their footprints in retail markets, so as not to hurt local groceries, including 
vendors of vegetables and fruits; 
Article II.  if so, the decisions taken in the matter to protect the interests of small retailers 
and consumers; and 
Article III.  the steps taken and the directions issued by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION 
(SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement  
(a) The retailers/traders register their shops with concerned authorities in various States. 
Presently, there is no restriction on the entry of any domestic investor into retail sector. So far as 
Foreign Direct Investment is concerned, as per extant policy, the Government allows 100 per cent 
foreign direct investment (FDI) in cash and carry through the automatic routs and 51 per cent in 
single brand.  
. (b) and (c) Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion have on 20-3-2007 sanctioned a 
Study on "The Impact of organized Retailing on the Unorganized Retail Sector" to be carried out 
by International Council for Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER). The Study 
will, inter alia, cover effect on organized retailing on small retail ers and vendors in the 
unorganized sector keeping in mind the likely growt h in the overall market and effect on 
employment. The recommendations and findings of this study will enable the Government to 
take a view on the need to have a policy on organized with regard to its overall impact. ICRIER 
was to submit the final Report in July, 2007 but has sought change in time schedule to enable 
additional survey for the study. The Final report by NCAER is scheduled to be submitted by 
May, 2008.  
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I refer to the reply, to what the hon. 
Minister has given. I will just quote the operative part of it. It says. "...the Government allows 
100 per cent FDI in cash and carry through the automatic route and 51 per cent in single brand." 
Then, in the second part he sayS, "The final Report by NCAER is scheduled to be submitted by 
May 2008." Does it mean to say that the Government has taken all these decisions about FDI, 
automatic route and in single brand even before getting the report? If it has already taken and the 
report says that the decision taken is not right, is it possible that the Government will be able to 
change it because those investments have already come to India? What is the importance of this 
kind of report being made now? That is one thing, Sir. In the

same sequence, I would like to know whether the Gov ernment has taken cognisance of the 
changing business model adopted by mega retail chains in the country, thereby involving the small 
retailer and local shops in their business model; if so, whether the Government encourages 
such business models.  
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, firstly, I think, the hon. Member seems to have some 
misunderstanding. The Government has not taken any decision to allow the FDI in retail sector. 
The Government is also not considering any such proposal, because we want to protect the 
interest of the retailers. Here, the ICRIER, has been deputed to do a particular job. It is supposed to 
study "The Impact of organised Retailing on the Unorganised Retail Sector." This organised 
retail is the domestic retail. Now, a number of big  companies are coming up and there is a 
general discussion. That is why, we have entrusted this task to ICRIER so that we can understand 
as to what is the impact of the domestic organised sector on the retailing. So, the question of 
FDI does not arise.  
Secondly, the Government cannot stop this. The Government of India has no authority. The 
State Government concerned is competent under the Shops and Establishments Act to take 
decision whether to allow opening a shop. So, all t he powers are vested with the State 
Government.  
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Sir, may be, I was confused.  I am happy that the hon. 
Minister has clarified it. But, what is the meaning of 51 per cent in a single brand? This is creating 
more confusion. Probably, I have not been able to understand. I would be grateful if the hon. 
Minister explains it further. It is because, 51 per cent or 99 per cent or 100 per cent is the same 
thing. If the Government is going to take a decision on this, it should be either for unlimited 
percentage or otherwise. This is wrong to misguide the nation that we are allowing only 51 per cent. 
That is neither here nor there. Sir, there is so much opposition in the minds of the individuals.  
The Economic Survey of this year says that the Government intends to open up the retail sector 
for FDI. This is what the Economic Survey says. it is there. If it is not there, it is well and good. 
So, how does the Government intend to attract FDI in view of the domestic opposition? If that 
happens, does the Government have any plan to change the Acts like AMPC, Shops and 
Establishments, accordingly?  
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, I have made the position absolutely clear that there is no 
proposal and the Government is not thinking to allow FDI in retail sector. We want to protect the 
interest of the retailers in this country.  
SHRI ARJUN KUMAR SENGUPTA: Sir, this is a very major question. I must say that the 
reply of the hon. Minister is rather unsatisfactory. He admits that there is FDI in cash and 51 per cent 
otherwise in single brand. The question that Mr. Bagrodia asked is whether the Government is 
considering any policy to protect the retail traders as a result of this kind of change in policy. It is a 
fact, I must say, that the Economic Survey has said exactly what Mr. Bagrodia is saying. If the hon. 
Minister says that this is not the policy of the Government, it is very good. But, nobody knows that 
the Economic Survey is saying something which is not the Government's policy. But the question 
is: what is the Government doing? What policy are they, actually, adopting to protect the small 
retailers? Sir, the member says that the ICRIER is preparing a study. I have seen the studies that have 
been done by it before. This is not an answer. The answer is that the Government must take a 
view of the whole policy itself. By the way, there is a mistake in the reply. The last sentence is 
about NCAER. The NCAER is not involved in this.

Rail accidents in the country  
*225. DR. V. MAITREYAN: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state:  
1)  the total number of rail accidents reported across the country during the last year; 
2)  the total loss of life and property due to these accidents; 
3)  the compensation paid to the affected families of the deceased in these accidents; 
4)  whether it is a fact that many cases of compensation are still pending in the Ministry 
and if so, how they are likely to be disposed of; 
5)  what are the reasons for these tragedies reported; 
6)  how many persons in the Ministry found negligent in  duties have been brought to 
book; and 
7)  what steps are being taken to prevent such accidents in future? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. VELU): 
(a) to (g) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement  
(a) to (c) There were 195 consequential train accidents on Indian Railways during 2006-
07 in which 208 persons lost their lives and 402 sustained injuries. Loss of railway property 
on account of these accidents has been estimated to  be Rs. 31.93 crore. Compensation is 
paid only after a decree is awarded on a claim file d in this regard in the Railway Claims 
Tribunal. So far Rs. 36 lakhs have been paid as compensation for claims filed in respect of 
these accidents.  
1.  No, Sir. Accident compensation claims are adjudicated by Railway Claims Tribunal 
which is a quasi judicial body. However, Railways have taken steps to speed up settlement 
of compensation claims. 
2.  and (f) Out of 195 consequential train accidents during 2006-07,85 were attributed to 
failure of railway staff, 84 due to failure of persons other that railway staff, 9 due to equipment 
failure, 8 due to sabotage, 7 were incdental, 1 due to combination of factors and I could not 
be established. During 2006-07, disciplinary action was taken against 200 railway employees 
held responsible for accidents. 
(g) All possible steps are undertaken on a continui ng basis to prevent accidents. These 
measures include timely replacement of over-aged assets, adoption of suitable technologies 
for up-gradation and maintenance of track, rolling stock, signaling and interlocking systems, 
safety drives and inspections at regular intervals to monitor and educate staff for observance 
of safe practices. As a result, there has been a de clining trend in the number of accidents 
from 473 in 2000-01 to 234 in 2005-06 and further to 195 in 2006-07.  
DR. V. MAITREYAN: Mr. Chairman, the reply by the Minister shows that a large number 
of rail accidents occur due to human errors. In fact, 169 out of 195 accidents occurred due to

human error. But, there is no mention about the num ber of accidents that occurred due to 
unmanned level crossings. What is the total number of unmanned level crossings across the 
country, and, in Tamil Nadu in particular? What is the number of accidents occurring due to these 
unmanned level crossings in the country and in Tamil Nadu? I want to know the number of 
overbridges that are being contemplated to be built this year across the country and in Tamil 
Nadu. What steps is the Ministry going to undertake to check these accidents which occur due to 
these unmanned level crossings?  
SHRIR. VELU: Sir, I quite agree and share the concern of the hon. Member. Today, the 
problem faced by the Railways, especially, in respect of accidents is of the unmanned level 
corssings. We have about 34,000 level crossings, of  which 16,000 and odd are manned 
crossings and about 18,000 are unmanned level corssings.  
Sir, as I mentioned, these unmanned level crossings are causing concern. But we have now 
evolved a policy to see to it that unmanned level crossings are increasingly manned. This is 
number one. We have also, according to the volume of traffic, provided for grade separators, 
namely, ROB and RUB. On the remaioning unmanned level crossings, we are now applying the 
visibility criteria and we are also providing for manning of those eligible crossings. Sir, for 
manning, the capital cost works out to about Rs.10 to 12 lakh and the operating cost for every 
crossing works out to three lakh of rupees per annum. If I want to convert all of them into manned 
crossings, I need about Rs. 2156 crore as capital cost, and, to run them, to man them, the recurring 
cost works out to about 539 crores of rupees a year.  
DR. V. MAITREYAN: Sir, there is a surplus of Rs. 25 ,000 crores. ...(Interruptions).... 
There is a surplus.  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Just a minute. Let him finish.  
SHRI R. VELU: Sir, 36 per cent of the accidents in India take place on the unmanned level 
crossings, but, if you take the fatalities also into account, 70 per cent of the fatalities are there on 
the unmanned level crossing. So, what we are doing is, in all those places, we are upgrading the 
infrastructural facilities namely, grading, rumbling, improving whistling by drivers, train-warning 
systems so that the road-user is cautioned. We are doing all these things. Now, as far as this 
particular question of the hon. Member regarding the number of manned and unmanned crossings 
in Tamil Nadu and the efforts that are being made to stop these accidents, etc. are concerned, I will 
furnish the information to the hon. Member separately.  
DR. V. MAITREYAN: Sir, the reply of the hon. Minister mentions that the large number of 
accidents occur due to human erros. My question is: how many of them are due to human error and 
how many of them are due to human negligence? And, whether the Government will propose to 
appoint a Committee to study this aspect and give suggestions so that the field staff can be 
trained to handle these things in a more human way. 
SHRI R. VELU: Sir, the percentage of accidents caused due to human error on the part of the 
Railway staff constitutes about 43.59 per cent. ...(Interruptions)....

SHRI R. VELU: Sir, as far as the question regarding  failure on the part of the Railway 
staff is concerned, I would like to say that at the level of the recruitment itself, we are taking 
all kinds of aptitude tests, etc., so that the right persons are selected. Even after recruitment, 
a number of training courses at the induction level as well as refresher courses at periodical 
intervals are conducted. Various other measures are also being undertaken so that the running 
staff is not negligent of their duties and to see that the skill and performance of the Railway 
staff is all the time upgraded so that such accidents do not occur. For the people other than 
the Railway staff, that is, the road users and othe rs we undertake awareness campaigns to 
make them how to cross the unmanned level corssings. In fact, the Motor Vehicle Act provides 
certain guidelines to be observed by the drivers. But they do not observe them. That is why 
these accidents take place. So, we are taking aggressive campaigns to educate the people to 
make them aware. So, in this way we are trying to m inimise the number of accidents on 
account of human failure on the part of Railways as well as the non-railway side.  
DR. K. MALAISAMY: Sir, I feel at home with the Chairman as well as the Minister. It is 
very much gratifying to note that the number of accidents is coming down. From the report, 
we see that the total number accidents is coming down. While we are happy on that aspect,  

Oral Answers  [14 MARCH 2008]  to Questions    17  
it is also seen from the report that about 80-90 per cent of the accidents are due to human failure, 
not because of mechanical failure or other things. If most of the accidents are because of human 
failure, I would like the Ministry to have more and more thrust and concentration on the persons 
who are involved in human failure. The Minister is saying that they are concentrating on that 
aspect. On the other hand, there are no all-out efforts to train them, to educate them, to create 
awareness among them. What is the real thrust that you are giving to reduce the number of 
accidents, mainly concentrating on the human area?  
SHRIR. VELU: Sir, the hon. Member has rightly pointed out that the number of accidents has 
come down. The number of accidents, which were 415 in 2001-02, had drastrically come down 
to 195 during the last year, that is, 2006-07, and, this year, at the end of February, the number was 
184. This is all because of upgradation in technology and upgradation of human resources. I have 
already mentioned how we are going to tackle the si tuation by improving the quality of 
recruitment, undertaking referesher courses and crash courses, modernising the training refresher 
courses and crash courses, modernising the training centres, undertaking periodical medical 
examinations, introducing breathalysers, computerised management filling the vacancies in the 
'safety' category on priority, etc., etc. So, a num ber of measures are being taken. But the 
uncontrollable factor is the public, the road users. As I mentioned just noW, we are undertaking 
awareness programmes to educate them. This is not the problem in India alone. It is a universal 
problem. We do not find anywhere in the world a foolproof system in which the unmanned level 
crossings will not be subject to accidents unless people are made aware how seriously they should 
cross the unmanned level crossings. However, the number of such accidents has come down. Of 
course, zero level may not be possible, but, at least, we can try to reduce the number of accidents.  
SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Sir, I would like to know whether the hon. Railway Minister is 
aware of the fact that after every major disaster a Commission is appointed. If you take into 
account all the recommendations, made by such commissions, they are about 2,200. One of the 
main proposals is to modernise the railway safety system with updated technology. I would like to 
know from the Minister, out of those 2,200 recommendations, how many recommendations 
have been implemented to avoid the train disasters. 
SHRI R. VELU: Sir, many Committees like the Wanchoo Committee and all others have gone 
into this aspect. The latest was the Railway Safety Review Committee, appointed in 1998. It 
was headed by Justice Khanna. In fact he had made about 278 recommendations. Of course, the 
hon. Member wants the details of the 2,200 recommendations, which were made over a period of 
about 60 years. I will definitely furnish this information to him. But the latest being this, out of 
278 recommendations, the Railways has accepted 240 of them. (Interruptions) What I am 
saying is that I will definitely furnish those particulars. But I would like to inform about the 
latest recommendations, which are under operation. So, out of 278" recommendations, 240 have 
been accepted, 198 have been implemented, and 38 recommendations have not been accepted. 
And this Safety Review Committee is responsible for improvement in safety. Out of Rs. 17,000 
crores, Rs. 12,000 crores will be from the Finance Minister and Rs. 5,000 crores from the 
Railways. This has been helping us to upgrade our track structure, rolling stock, signalling, etc., 
which has been responsible for the drastic reduction in accidents. I shall furnish the other details 
that he wanted, Sir.  
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Sir, my question relates to part (e) of the reply of the hon. 
Minister; and, in view of its importance, I would have appreciated had the hon. Railway Minister 
himself been present. You have talked to all the new technology you are seeking to  

18   Oral Answers  [RAJYA SABHA]  to Questions  
adopt to prevent railway accidents. There has been a provision of a big Railway Safety Fund. 
How has that Fund been utilised? That is my first q uestion. Secondly, you have liberalised 
freight load on freight trains; that would lead to impact on the tracks. How are you going to take 
care of that? Is overload on the track a problem giving rise to accidents? These are my two 
queries to which I wish to seek answers.  
SHRI R. VELU: Sir, these are good questions put by the hon. Member and I would definitely 
like to inform him. Sir, so far as the Railway Safety Fund is concerned, this will be utilised for 
replacement and renewal of 16538 kilometres of railway track of which we have done about 
16223 kms., that is, about 98 per cent of it has been done. Then, 2286 bridges will be renewed 
and reconstructed. We have done 2087, that is, about 91.2 per cent of the work has been done. 
As for signalling, signals at 1448 stations were needed to be done, of which 1222 have been 
done, that is, 77 per cent of the work has been don e. We were given a six-year period for 
completion but some work remained to be completed and so one year more was given. So, by 
the end of this year, we will be able to complete almost the entire renewal work as well as utilise 
the funds. Then, you have raised a query about increase in the axle load having an impact on the 
track and how much of the safety aspect is being ta ken care of. In fact, when we thought of 
increasing the axle load, we took care by not straightaway implementing it but gave it a trial run of 
six months on those routes where we had got increased load, which means, the carrying capacity 
plus 6+2 or CC+8+2 is the increased axle load, the additional weight and tonnage which has to 
be carried. We found that the tracks and the bridges could bear it and mat is why we have put it 
into operation. The point is that we in the Railways do not care for the income but for the safety of 
the passengers as well as the safety of the goods. I assure the hon. Member that we will not take 
such a hasty step in introducing the additional wei ght without taking care of the renewal, 
replacement of the tracks, the rolling stock bridges, etc.

†*226. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI:  
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI:tt  
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state:  
1)  whether it is a fact that the consumer sale price of steel has been on continuous rise in 
the country during the past years; 
2)  if so, the average prices of different varieties of steel in the country during April, 2004 
and at the end of December, 2007; and 
3)  to what extent the prices of all material used in steel manufacturing have increased 
during the said period  ?t  Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

whether Government is aware of the fact that the demand for the steel commodity is      growing

whether Government has taken any steps to bridge the gap between demand and supply of this

Sale of gender identification kits  
*228. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: 
SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR:  
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:  
1)  whether it is a fact that gender identification kits are available for sale by a US based 
company through a website; and 
2)  if so, the steps Government is contemplating either to ban the website in the country or 
regulate its sale in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) The declining sex ratio is a matter of great concern and calls for 
concerted action from all quarters. In order to con tain the menace of female foeticide and 
ushering in a healthy sex ratio in the Country, the Central Government enacted the Preconception 
and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994. The Act, inter alia, provides for stringent 
action against individuals and genetic laboratories /clinics offering sex determination 
services. Similar penalty provision also exists for those who seek such services.  
1)  Various mechanisms have been evolved at the national, State and district levels to ensure 
strict compliance of the provisions of the Act by all stake holders through periodic inspection 
and monitoring. 
2)  The advent of internet e-communication has emerged as a new threat in this regard. It has 
been reported that some of the overseas agencies are freely posting advertisements pertaining to 
sex determination services and wares. For instance, web sites like the •www.GenSelect.com ; 
www.4-gender-selection.com , www.pregnancystore.com , etc., are offering sex determination 
kits called the'baby Gender Mentor Home DNA Test Kit', that 

Written Answers to  [14 MARCH 2008]  Starred Questions   25  
help the buyer determine the sex of the foetus through DNA analysis at home.  
1)  The matter was referred to the Ministry of Communications and IT to block the offending 
websites. But, mat Ministry expressed the view that such an action did not render the promoters of such 
sites completely ineffective as they could re-emerge and be available for the viewers again under 
a new nomenclature and in a new avatar. 
2)  To identify the people involved, the issue was then  taken up with the Department of 
Revenue, Ministry of Finance, to trap the people importing the sex determination kits pandered by the 
offending overseas websites into the Country. 
3)  The Ministry of Health requested the Customs Department for details of the individuals ir 
organisations who have imported the sex determination (Gender Testing)kits from abroad to 
facilitate the Government to proceed further against such people under Section 23 (3) of the PC & 
PNDT Act and also to intercept and not release such articles under Sub-Section (2) (k), (u) and 
(v) of Section 11 under Chapter IV of the Customs A ct, 1962 (52 of 1962), vide the 
Government's letter dated 29.11.2007 and 5.1.2008. 
4)  In response to the Government's above request, the Customs Department have suitably alerted 
their field formations not to release the imported Gender Testing Kits and to take appropriate 
action under the Customs Act. 
Disabilities due to alcohol consumption  
*229. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA:  
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:  
1)  whether Government is aware that consumption of alc ohol is ruining the health of 
millions of young people in the country; 
(b)  if so, the details thereof; 
(c)  whether alcoholism is creating host of diseases and disabilities in people; 
2)  whether Government proposes to take some tough decisions to check alcoholism in the 
country; and 
(d)  if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) to (e) The Government is cognizant of the fact that consumption of alcohol in 
excessive amounts can lead to social, economic and health related problems. A study conduced 
by NIMHANS for WHO published in the year 2006 shows that nearly 30% of adult men and less 
than 5% of women consume alcohol giving a male to female ratio of 6:1. Alcohol use is higher in 
poor communities. The average age of initiation has reduced from 28 years during the 80s to 
20 years in recent years.  
Alcoholism could lead to liver disease and brain damage, gastro intestinal diseases, peptic ulcer, 
pancreatic diseases, nervous system related diseases, alcoholic dementia, alcoholic memory 
loss, peripheral nerve damage, muscle damage, cancer of several body organs, hypertension 
and coronary heart diseases etc. Besides severe health problems, accidents also take place 
resulting in head injuries and hospitalizations.

The policy with regard to sale and distribution of alcohol is within the purview of the 
State Governments. Therefore, the efforts made to c ontain the damage done by alcoholism 
vary from State to State. The business of alcohol i s a controlled one and without a licence 
issued by the respective State Government, no one c an sell alcoholic beverages. Selling of 
alcoholic beverages to minors is prohibited. A high  rate of State excise duty is levied to 
dissuade people from consuming alcohol. Advertisements of alcoholic beverages have been 
banned by the Government.  
Apart from this, clinical care, building awareness, counselling and rehabilitation is made 
available through de-addiction centres and counselling centres run/funded by the Government.

Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether WHO in its first report on global tobacco use and control efforts, has revealed 
that the use of tobacco by young women in India is rapidly increasing; 
(b)  if so, the facts and the details thereof; 
(c)  whether the steps taken by Government to control use of tobacco by citizens have not

which is affecting the lives of citizens? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) to (d) WHO report on Global Tobacco Epidemic 2008, has revealed rise in 
tobacco use among young women in high population countries. The report has projected the 
trend having portents of an ominous potential of an epidemic. The report also indicates that 
women smoke at about one fourth rate of men and tobacco industry is aggressively marketing 
to tap this potential. As per NFHS-3, data published in 2007,10.8% Women in India consume 
some form of tobacco.  
Government of India has enacted a strong Tobacco Co ntrol Act, namely The Cigarettes 
and Other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertis ement and Regulation of Trade and 
Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act,  2003, which provides for the 
following:—  
2.  Prohibition of direct and indirect advertisement of all tobacco products. 
3.  Prohibition of smoking in a public place. 
4.  Prohibition of sale of all tobacco products to a person below the age of 18 years. 
5.  Prohibition of sale of all tobacco products within a radius of 100 yards of educational 
institutions. 
 Mandatory depiction of statutory warning (includin g pictorial warnings) on tobacco 
packs.  
> Regulation of Nicotine and Tar Content (yet to be  enforced).

Herbal treatment  
t*231. SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: SHRI 
RAM JETHMALANI:  
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether it is a fact that treatment with herbs has been found effective in the country; 
(c)  whether it is also a fact that treatment through aforesaid system is cheaper as well as easy; 
(b)  if so, the reaction of Government thereto; and 
(d)  whether Government has formulated any scheme to make this system of medicine more 
effective and if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) to (d) Ayurveda, Yoga, Siddha and Unani are ancient but holistic healthcare 
systems with proven efficacy for treatment of various disorders.  
There is global resurgence of interest in traditional medicinal systems and herbal remedies all over 
the world including India. National Health Policy, 1983, suggested initiation of measures to 
enable various systems of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy to be developed in accordance with 
their genius and their integration at the appropriate levels, within specified areas of responsibility and 
functioning in the overall healthcare delivery systems, especially in regard to the preventive, 
promotive and public health objectives.  
In accordance with these objectives, Government of India has provided full support for the 
development of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoe opathy. Pharmacopoeia 
Committees, Pharmacopoeia! Laboratories, Research Institutions and National Institutes have been set 
up for Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy systems. Various Central 
Sector and Centrally Sponsored Schemes have been initiated for laying down of pharmacopoeial 
standards, standardization and quality control of AYUSH products, development and upgradation of 
AYUSH education. In addition to research by AYUSH Research Councils, research under Extra 
Mural Research Projects and Golden Triangle Partnership Projects on traditional medicine have 
been launched by Department of AYUSH in collaboration with CSIR and JCMR for scientific 
validation of AYUSH drugs and drugless therapies. Assistance is also being provided to State 
Governments for opening of AYUSH units at the Distr ict Hospital/CHCs/PHCs level for 
integration of AYUSH in national healthcare delivery.  
National Medicinal Plants Board has also been set u p to promote cultivation and 
conservation of medicinal plants. New initiatives have been launched in the Eleventh Plan for 
providing assistance to Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy manufacturing units to 
establish in-house quality control laboratories and setting up of common facilities for AYUSH 
industry clusters, assistance to centres of excellence engaged in AYUSH research, public health 
and revitalization of local health traditions.

Decline in female foeticide  
†*232. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of HEALT H AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state:  
(c)  whether the cases of female foeticide have declined after the formulation of strict rules 
and law and if so, the figures of last three years in this regard, State-wise and year-wise; 
(d)  which are the States where majority of incidents of female foeticide are happening and 
the reasons therefor; and 
(e)  the names of States where the percentage of female is lower than that of male due to 
female foeticide, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) Sex ratio (number of females per thousand males) is one of the most 
important indicator used for study of population characteristics. Declining trend in sex ratio has 
been a matter of concern for all in the country. Sex ratio in India has declined over the century from 
972 in 1901 to 927 in 1991. The sex ratio has since gone up to 933 in 2001.  
In contrast, the child sex ratio for the age group of 0-6 years in 2001 is 927 girls per 
thousand boys against 945 recorded in 1991 Census. The encouraging trend in the sex ratio during 
1991—2001 was marred by the decline of 18 points in the sex ratio of children aged 6 years or 
below.  
The Census 2001 figures further reveal that the child sex ratio is comparatively lower in the 
affluent regions, i.e., Punjab (798), Haryana (819), Chandigarh (845), Delhi (868), Gujarat (883) and 
Himachal Pradesh (896). State/UT-wise sex ratio and child sex ratio as per 1991 and 2001 
Census is at Statement-I (See below).  
The number of foeticides (male+female) between the years 2004-2006 is at Statement-ii (See 
below). Cases of total foeticide have increased in 2006 as compared to the years 2005 and 2004.  
The National Crime Record Bureau (NCRB) have furnished the following information:  
The three States/UTs with the maximum number of cases registered under foeticide (male + 
female) during each of the years 2004—2006

Some of the reasons commonly put forward to explain the consistently low levels of sex ratio 
are son preference, neglect of the girl child resulting in higher mortality at younger age, female 
infanticide, female foeticide, higher maternal mortality and male bias in enumeration of population. 
Easy availability of sex determination test and abortion services may also be providing to be 
catalyst in the process, which may be further stimu lated by pre-conception sex selection 
facilities.  
Sex determination techniques have been in use in In dia since 1975 primarily for the 
determination of genetic abnormalities. However, these techniques were widely misused to 
determine the sex of the foetus and subsequent abortions if the foetus was found to be female.

In order to check female foeticide, the Pre-natal D iagnostic Techniques (Regulation and 
Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994, was brought into operation from 1st January, 1996. The Pre-
natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994 has since been 
amended to make it more comprehensive. The amended Act and Rules came into force with effect 
from 14.2.2003 and the PNDT Act has been renamed as "Pre-conception and Pre-natal 
Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection ) Act, 1994" to make it more 
comprehensive.  
The technique of pre-conception sex selection has been brought within the ambit of this Act 
so as to pre-empt the use of such technologies, which significantly contribute to the declining 
sex ratio. Use of ultrasound machines has also been brought within the purview of this Act more 
explicitly so as to curb their misuse for detection and disclosure of sex of the foetus lest it should 
lead to female foeticide. The Central Supervisory Board (CSB) constituted under the Chairmanship 
of Minister for Health and Family Welfare has been further empowered for monitoring the 
implementation of the Act. State level Supervisory Boards in the line of the CSB constituted at the 
Centre has been introduced for monitoring and reviewing the implementation of the Act in States/UTs. 
The State/UT level Appropriate Authority have been made a multi member body for better 
implementation and monitoring of the Act in the States. More stringent punishments are prescribed 
under the Act so as to serve as a deterrent for min imizing violations of the Act Appropriate 
Authorities are empowered with the powers of Civil Court for search, seizure and sealing the 
machines, equipments and records of the violators of law including sealing of premises and 
commissioning of witnesses. It has been made mandatory to maintain proper records in respect of 
the use of ultrasound machines and other equipments capable of detection of sex of foetus and 
also in respect of tests and procedures that may lead to pre-conception selection of sex. The sale of 
ultrasound machines has been regulated through laying down the condition of sale only to the 
bodies registered under the Act.  
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has taken a number of steps for the implementation of the 
Act, IEC activities for generating awareness among the public about the debilitating impact of 
skewed sex ratio on the society, sensitization/training of the implementing agencies, including the 
lower judiciary and the Public Prosecutors.  
It is hoped that the sincere effort with which the PC and PNDT Act is being implemented, would 
make lead to an improvement in the child sex ratio. However, a confirmation of this would be 
known only after the 2011 Census.

Organic Manure  
1553. SHRI MATI JAYA BACHCHAN: Will the Minister of  AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state:  
 whether Government has studied the effects of the organic manure; 
 if so, what are the findings; and 
 whether there is any mechanism to monitor its quality and if so, what are the details in 
this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E (SHRI 
KANTILABHURIA): (a) and (b) Under All India Coordinated Research Project (AICRP) on 
'long term fertilizer experiments' over the last fe w decades, Indian Council of Agriculture 
Research (ICAR) has concluded that only integrated use of optimal dose of Nitrogen, 
Phosphorous & Potash (NPK) and organic manure can maintain soil health and give higher 
sustainable yields. Organic manure, besides supplyi ng essential plant nutrients, improves 
soil physical conditions and stimulates biological activities of soils through supply of energy 
to soil microbes.  
(c) Organic manures are mostly produced on farm and  used by the farmers. However, 
with commercialization of few type of organic manur es, three organic manures have been 
brought under Fertilizer Control Order (FCO) namely  (i) City waste compost (ii) Vermi-
compost and (iii) Press-mud. The quality of the abo ve organic manure is monitored as per 
the specifications/provisions of FCO.

Checking the poultry rearing in country yards  
1554. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRALAH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased 
to state:  
 in the light of repeated emergence of bird-flue thr eats in the country whether 
Government in coordination with World Health Organi zation (WHO) and other affected 
neighbouring countries is taking any steps to incul cate best practices while simultaneously 
initiating steps to discourage the practice of rear ing poultries in the backyard of rural 
households; 
 if so, the details of steps taken towards the said two fronts; and 
 if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E (SHRI 
KANTILALBHURIA): (a) and (b) Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) has adopted 
WHO recommended guidelines for managing human cases of Avian Influenza and pandemic 
preparedness.  
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has proposed cross-border surveillance for 
Avian Influenza involving India, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Nepal in order to have transparency, 
exchange of bird flue related information, trade in livestock products and mutual cooperation in 
control and containment of Avian Influenza. The proposal has been agreed to in-principle.  
• An Information, Education and Communication (IEC) campaign has been launched in print 
media and over television and radio. The campaign h as focused on safe poultry practices, 
preparedness, food safety implications and consuming well cooked chicken and eggs. The 
poultry industry is also encouraged to carry out similar campaign.  
(c) Question does not arise.  
Implementation of Swaminathan Committee Report  
1555. SHRI SITARAM YECHURY: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state:  
 whether it is a fact that the Swaminathan Committee recommended several steps for the 
revival of agriculture; 
 if so, the salient features of the recommendations; 
 the details  of the progress of implementation, recommendation-wise; 
 whether it is also a fact that implementation of recommendations is not up to the expected 
level; 
 if so, the reasons therefor; and 
 the steps contemplated by Government to implement the above said recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) Yes, Sir.  
(b) to (f) Based on the recommendations of the National Commission on Farmers headed by 
Prof. M.S. Swaminathan, as contained in the Revised Draft National Policy for Farmers,  

Written Answers to  [14 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions 5 1 
submitted by the Commission, the Government has approved the National Policy for Fanners 
2007 which has also been laid on the Table of the H ouse in November 2007. Various 
recommendations made by the Commission for revival of agriculture and allied sectors, as 
accepted by the Government, have been incorporated in the National Policy for Farmers.  
These include, inter alia, asset reforms in respect of land, water, livestock,  fisheries and 
bioresources; support services and inputs like application of frontier technologies; agricultural 
biosecurity system; supply of good quality seeds an d disease-free planting material; issue of 
soil health passbooks to the farmers and integrated  pest management system; region and 
'crop specific implements and machinery; support se rvices for women like creches, child 
care centres, nutrition, health and training; timel y, adequate and easy reach of institutional 
credit at reasonable interest rates and farmer-friendly insurance instruments; use of Information 
and Communication Technology and setting up of farm  schools to revitalize agricultural 
extension; coverage of farmers under a comprehensiv e national social security scheme; 
effective implementation of MSP across the country and establishing community foodgrain 
banks development of agricultural market infrastructure and terminal markets for agriculture; 
curriculum reforms in agricultural universities; sp ecial categories of farming like organic 
farming and contract farming; rural non-farm employ ment initiative for farm households; 
and integrated approach for rural energy, etc.  
A very few recommendations of NCF contained in the Revised Draft National Policy for 
Farmers have not been incorporated in the National Policy for Farmers 2007. These include, 
inter alia, (i) fixation of Minimum Support Price (MSP) at least 50% higher than the weighted ' 
average cost of production — as MSP is recommended by the Commission for Agricultural 
Costs & Prices (CACP) on objective criteria conside ring variety of relevant factors and a 
mechanical linkage betwen MSP and cost of productio n may be counter-productive; (ii) 
Public Distribution System (PDS) to be made univers al — as PDS is a targeted scheme 
where even off take for BPL families is short again st allocation for BPL categories; (iii) 
establishment of Indian Trade Organisation and National Livestock Development Council at the 
National level — as the concerned Departments of Go vernment of India opposed to their 
establishment; (iv) setting up of Agricultural Risk Fund, Market Price Stabilisation Fund and 
Gram Panchayat Mahila Fund — as Ministry of Finance  opined that these should be proposed 
as schemes to be funded through the normal budgeting process.  
Many of the provisions contained in the National Po licy for Farmers 2007 are already 
under implementation by various Central Ministries and Departments and the States through 
several on-going schemes and programmes. These incl ude, inter-alia, Bharat Nirman for 
improving rural infrastructure and irrigation potential; National Rural Employment Guarantee 
Scheme carrying a legal guarantee of employment; Sw aranjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana 
to promote self-employment among the rural poor; Na tional Rural Health Mission; 
Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme to complet e more irrigation projects; pilot 
projects to repair, renovate and restore water bodi es and groundwater recharge programme 
to divert rainwater into dug-wells; revival of agricul tural extension system, reforms in 
agricultural marketing and development of market in frastructure; establishment of National 
Horticulture Mission, National Rainfed Area Authori ty, National Fisheries Development 
Board, National Bamboo Mission, etc.; expansion of institutional farm credit at reduced 
rate of interests; Rural Infrastructure Development  Fund; Rajeev Gandhi Grameen 
Vidyutikaran Yojana; and several other initiatives.  Government of India has recently 
launched two new schemes i.e. National Food Security Mission to improve production  
and productivity of foodgrains and Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana to incentivize States to

Slow pace in Agricultural Sector  
1561. DR. M.A.M. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state:  
 whether the foodgrains output in the country is growing at less than 3 per cent every 
year; 
 if so, the reasons for this slow pace of output in agricultural sector; 
 whether it is a fact the production of foodgrains and pulses have been stagnated for a 
number of years; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 the reasons therefor; and 
 the steps taken by the Central Government to make farming attractive? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) The growth in the foo dgrains output has been 
fluctuating over the year. The foodgrains output in the country grew at 5.2 per cent during 
2005-06, at 4.2 per cent during 2006-07 and is esti mated to grow at 0.9 per cent during 
2007-08.  
The annual foodgrains output depends upon a combination of factors like temporal and 
spatial distribution of monsoon rainfall, timely av ailability and use of quality seeds and 
fertilizers, incidence of pests and diseases and irrigation facility; among others.  
(c) to (e) During the last ten years, the foodgrain s production has increased from 
203.61 million tonnes during 1998-99 to 219.32 mill ion tonnes during 2007-08 (2nd 
advance estimates released on 7th February 2008). H owever, the production of pulses 
was 14.91 million tonnes during 1998-99 and is esti mated to be 14.34 million tonnes 
during 2007-08.  
The reasons for stagnation in the production of pul ses are: Pulses are genetically low 
yielding and less input responsive as compared to c ereals, the cultivation of pulses is done 
on marginal and sub-marginal land under rainfed conditions by small and marginal farmers 
whose capacity for input use is very low, there is no varietal break-through and pulses are 
more prone to pests and diseases.  
(0 Government has approved the National Policy for Fanners 2007, which inter-alia 
aims to improve the economic viability of farming by substantially increasing the net income

support services and inputs like application of frontier technologies for improving productivity, 
supply of good quality seeds and disease free planting material, issue of soil health pass book and 
integrated nutrient and pest management system, among others. Further, Government has launched two 
new schemes (i) National Food Security Mission for increasing production and productivity of rice, 
wheat and pulses; and (ii) Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana to incentivise the States to increase public 
investment in Agriculture and Allied Sector. Besides, a Number of initiatives, Plan Schemes and

†l562.  SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: DR. 
MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI:  
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state:  
 whether the efforts of increasing the rate of yield of agriculture are being made in the 
country during the last few years; 
 if so, the details thereof; and 
 the estimated rate of yield of agriculture production in the country in the year 2003-2004 
and 2007-2008? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) Department of Agriculture & Cooperation is implementing 
a number of Plan Schemes for increasing the production, productivity, and rate of yield of 
agriculture. The measures taken under the said schemes include soil testing, availability of 
quality/high-yielding seeds, balanced and judicious use of chemical fertilizers in conjunction 
with organic sources of nutrients, pest management availability of water, etc. Ministry of 
Agriculture has recently launched two new schemes i.e. National Food Security Mission to 
improve production and productivity of rice, wheat and pulses and Rashtriya Krishi Vikas 
Yojana to incentivise the states to increase public investment in agriculture and allied sectors 
and to maximize returns to the farmers in agriculture and allied sector.  
(c) The details indicating All India Estimate of Area, Production and Yield of Foodgrains and 
Oilseeds for last five years are given in Statement—I and II.

Statement  
Details of scheme of Debt Waiver and Debt Relief for farmers  
A scheme of Debt Waiver and Debt Relief for farmers has been announced in the Union ,  
Budget 2008-09. The salient features of the propose d scheme are:  
(i) All agricultural loans disbursed by scheduled commercial banks, regional rural banks 
and cooperative credit institutions up to March 31,2007 and overdue as on December 
31,2007 will be covered under the scheme.  
(ii) For marginal farmers {i.e. holding upto 1 hectare) and small formers (1-2 hectare), there 
will be a complete waiver of all loans that were overdue on December 31, 2007 and 
which remained unpaid until February 29,2008. In respect of other farmers, there will be 
a One Time Settlement (OTS) scheme for all loans that were overdue on December 31, 
2007 and which remained unpaid until, February 29,2008. Under the OTS, a rebate of 
25 per cent will be given against payment of the balance of 75 per cent.  
(iii) Agricultural loans which were restructured an d rescheduled by banks in 2004 and 
2006 through special packages and other loans rescheduled in the normal course as per 
RBI guidelines, will also be eligible either for a waiver or OTS on the same pattern.  
(iv) The implementation of the debt waiver and debt relief scheme will be completed by 
June 30, 2008. Upon being granted debt waiver or si gning an agreement for debt 
relief under the OTS, the farmer would be entitled to fresh agricultural loans from 
the banks in accordance with normal rules.  
(v) It is estimated that about 3 crore small and marginal farmers and about 1 crore other  
farmers will be benefited under the proposed scheme. The total value of overdue  
loans being waived is estimated at Rs. 50,000 crore and the OTS relief on the overdue  
" loans is estimated at Rs. 10,000 crore.  * 
2. Considering that high rates of interest often act as a deterrnt to fanners from availing 
farm credit, it was announced in the Union Budget (2006-07), that crop loans upto Rs.3 lakh 
would be given at 7% rate of interest. Accordingly, crop loans are presently being made., 
available at 7% at the ground level by almost all banks with interest subvention from the 
Government of India. This scheme is continued for 2007-08 and 2008-09 also.

1566. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA:  
SHRI LALIT  KISHORE CHATURVEDI:  
Will  the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state:  
 whether India grows nearly 11 per cent of all the world's vegetables and 15 per cent of 
all fruits; 
 whether India's share in global market is only 1.7 per cent in vegetables and 0.5 per 
cent in fruit; 
 whether the Indian farmer receives less than a fifth of the high price that the consumer 
pays and the lion's share is usurped by the long ch ain of assorted middlemen, transport, 
wholesalers, and retailers who bring the produce from farm to market; 
     (d) if so, how pathetic is plight of farmer; and  
(e) the remedial steps being taken in this regard?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL * 
BHURIA ): (a) and (b) India Produces around 111.77 Million MT s of vegetables and 57.73 
million of MTs of fruits, which accounts for nearly  11.90 per cent and 10.90 per cent of 
country's share in the world production of vegetabl es and fruits, respectively. While the 
India' share in the global market in vegetables and fruits stands at 1.70 per cent and 0.50 per 
cent respectively. Details of production of vegetab les and fruits and export of horiticulture 
products are given in Statement I & II (See below).  

70    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
(c) to (e) Most of the agricultural commodity marke ts generally operate under the normal 
forces of demand and supply. The buying and selling of agricultural produce takes place in the 
market yards where numbers of market functionaries are involved. The share of producer in 
consumers price depend upon the types of marketing channels followed in sales transactions by 
the farmers. The studies indicate that the share of producers varies from 56 to 83 per cent « in 
food grains and 79 to 95 per cent in pulses, 65—96 per cent in oilseeds and 33 to 75 per cent 
in case of fruit and vegetables. In order to provide the remunerative prices to the farmers, there is 
a need to eliminate the chain of middlemen etc., by introducing innovative marketing channels 
like direct marketing, contract farming, etc. and removal of controls on movement and storage 
of agricultural produce across the country which wi ll facilitate functioning of common 
Indian market  
Keeping this in view, a Model Law on agricultural m arketing has been formulated by the 
inistry of Agriculture and circulated to all the St ates/Union Territories for making necessary 
amendment in their respective Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) Act in order to 
guide them in removal of legal barriers, which intr oduce inefficiencies and monopoly controls 
in the functioning of agricultural markets. It redefines the role of present Agricultural Produce 
Market Committee to promote alternative marketing s ystem, contract farming, direct 
marketing and farmers/consumers markets. Most of the State Governments have since initiated 
the process of amendment of APMC Act on the lines s uggested in the model law, which will 
facilitate competitive marketing. Since agriculture  marketing is a State subject, it is for the 
State Governments to amend the APMC Act, wherever r equired, to provide for , alternate 
marketing channels to the farmers through direct ma rketing, contract farming and setting up 
of markets in cooperative and private sector to ena ble him to decide the channel which 
provide him the best remunerative price for his agricultural produce.  
In addition, Ministry of Agriculture, Government of India is implementing two Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes namely "Technology Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture 
in North Eastern States, Sikkim, Jammu and Kashmir,  Himachal Pradesh and Uttaranchal" 
and "National Horticulture Mission" besides Schemes  on (i) Development of Commercial 
Horticulture through production and post harvest ma nagement and (ii) capital investment 
subsidy for construction/ expansion/modernization of cold storages/storage of horticultural 
produce of National Horticulture Board. Under the above mentioned schemes, assistance is 
being provided to State Governments and entrepreneu rs for development of infrastructure 
for post havrvest management and marketing of horti culture produce, which in turn help 
farmers in getting remunerative prices.  
Ministry of Agriculture is also implementing Market  Intervention Scheme (MIS) on the . 
request of State Governments/ Union Territories for  procurement of agricultural and 
horticultural commodities including red chilly gene rally perishable in nature. MIS is 
implemented in order to protect the growers of thes e commodities from making distress sale 
in the vent of bumper crop when there is glut in th e market and the prices tend to fall below 
economic levels/cost of production. Procurement is made by National Agricultural 
Cooperative Marketing Federation of India Ltd (NAFED) and State desinated agencies.  
Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Dev elopment Authority (APEDA), 
Ministry of Commerce has established 60 Agri Export Zones in the country for promotion of 
export of agricultural produce including furits and vegetables.

 whether it is a fact that public sector fertilizer companies including FACT are

 whether it is also a fact that various units of FACT are either closed or on the verge of 
shut down owing to the above reasons; 
 whether Government has taken/proposed to take comprehensive measures to overcome 
the crisis; and 
 if so, the details thereof?   
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND

1583. SHRI D. RAJA: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased 
to state:  
 whether he is aware of the Bhopal gas survivors' 85 0 km. padyatra from Bhopal to 
Delhi started in February, 2008; 
 what progress has been made by Government in meetin g the demands after their 1st

 the details of plans, to pin liability on Union Carbide Corporation for the contamination 
of groundwater and land in and around the factory site in Bhopal; 
 the steps taken by CBI to extradite former Union Carbide Chairman Warren Anderson 
to face trial in India; and 
 the steps taken by CBI to enforce Union Carbide Cor poration's appearance in the 
criminal case in the Bhopal Chief Judical Magistrate's court? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS 
(SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) Yes Sir.  
(b) Based on the sanction by the Government of India in April, 2006 for a project under 
the Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission, the State Government of Madhya

Circulation of banned pesticides and seeds  
1585. SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state:  
 whether it is a fact that some USA and Europe based agrochemical companies have 
had their products like pesticides and seeds banned in their own countries have found its 
way to India; 
 if so, the details thereof; and 
 the reasons for allowing such products in the Indian market? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) to (c) As per information made available by 
the Department of Agriculture and Cooperation no isolated information is available that 
some USA and Europe based agro-chemical companies had their product like pesticide 
banned in their own countries have found its way to India. However, some pesticides, which , 
are banned/severely restricted in other countries are permitted for use in our country. Their 
use has been permitted only after through reviews and satisfying that the particular pesticide 
does not pose harmful effect under the conditions of use in our country. Further, it is relevant 
to mention that the use of these pesticides is banned/restricted in one, two or few countries 
while their use is permitted in some other countries of the world. When it comes to the notice 
of the Government that a pesticide is banned in other country it gets the same reviewed for 
its continued use or otherwise in our country. Based on such reviews, 31 pesticides and their 
formulations have been banned Statement-1 (See below) and 12 have been restricted for use 
in the country Statement-II (See below). A list of pesticides banned/severely restricted in 
some other countries of the world but permitted for use in our country is at Statement-Ill 
(see below). The country permits the use of the insecticide based on its agro-climatic situations, 
crop pattern, geography, pest-disease-situation, ecology and socio-economic conditions.  
As regards circulation of banned seeds, the information is that Bt. Cotton is the only 
genetically modified crop approved for commercial cultivation in India Genetic Engineering 
Approval Committee (GEAC) of the Ministry of Environment & Forests, which is the 
competent authority under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. Bt. Cotton hybrids are under 
cultivation in nine States of the country namely Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya 
Pradesh, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. The area under Bt. 
Cotton has increased from 29,073 hectares in 2002-03 to 34.67 lakh hectares during 2006-
07 which is about 37.69% of the total cotton area in the country.  
The development of Bt. Cotton in USA set in motion the process for the cultivation of 
transgenic cotton. Bt. Cotton offers season long in plant protection against cotton's worst 
enemies — the bollworm complex of insects. Bt. Cotton is designed to reduce or eliminate 
the need to spray for bollworms. When bollworrms  feed on the Bt. Cotton plant, the Bt. 
Protein stops the larva from feeding further and causes its subsequent death. This self-defence 
system against bollworms heip farmers manages these pests in an effective manner with 
minimum use of chemicals. Bt. Cotton, however, does not control sucking pests. Bt. Cotton 
holds promise for enhancing cotton production.

Cry 1 Ac gene which is incorporated in cotton confers considerable amount of resistance 
to lepidopteron pests through the production of tox ins affecting the bollworms. The 
introduction of inbuilt resistance through these Bt. Genes results in reduction in insecticide 
application and enable better returns to the farmers.  
. In India, Maharashtra Hybrid Seeds Company (MAHYC O) first imported the parental 
cotton cultivar Coker 312 from Monsanto, USA and then carried out a contained breeding 
programme to incorporate the Bt. Gene into their el ite cotton inbred lines. The Bt. Cotton 
hybrids before their commercial approval in India w ere tested for their bio safety and 
environmental issues and thereafter released commercially for cultivation in six States in the 
Kharif 2002-03. The benefits of Bt. Cotton in India are in line with those enjoyed by farmers 
worldwide who have cultivated Bt. Cotton.

Shortage of fertilizers  
1586. SHRI SITARAM YECHURY: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILISERS be pleased to state:  
 whether it is a fact that the country is facing shortage of fertilizers for the forthcoming 
agricultural season; 
 the details of fertilizer production in the country since 2004 agricultural season, 
company-wise; 
 the details of demand between 2004 and 2007, fertilizer-wise; and 
 the steps contemplated by Government to bridge the gap between demand and supply 
of fertilizer? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) to (d) The company-wise production of 
major fertilizers like Urea, Di-Ammonium Phosphate (DAP) & Complex fertilizers 
(NPK) producing in the country since 2004-05 to 2007-08 is at Statement-I, II & III 
(See below).  
The assessed requirement of major fertilizers like Urea, DAP and Muriate of Potash 
(MOP) by the Department of Agriculture & Cooperation in the country during 2004-05 to 
2007-08 is at Statement-IV (See below).  
Government is encouraging industry to maximize indigenous production of fertilizers, 
particularly Urea, through necessary policy initiatives, subject to availability of gas. In respect 
of phosphatic fertilizers however, the country either imports fertilizer products like DAP or 
is substantially dependent on import of the required rock-phosphate/phosphoric acid for 
indigenous production. In so far as MOP is concerned, the entire requirement is met through 
imports.  
Imports of fertilizers are being made to meet the gap between requirement and indigenous 
production. While such imports in respect of Urea are canalized through State Trading 
Agencies like State Trading Corporation/MMTC Limited/Indian Potash Limited, that of 
decontrolled fertilizers like DAP & MOP are on Open General Licence (OGL). Adequate 
imports are being made to meet the requirement of farmers.

Diversion of PDS Grains 
1588. SHRIVUAY J. DARDA: 
DR. ABHISHEK MANU SINGHVI: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUB LIC DISTRIBUTION 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that during the last three  years PDS diversion worth Rs. 31,500 
crores has taken place; 
(b) if so, whether investigations have been made, cul prits booked and exemplary 
punishments given; 
(f)  whether the Planning Commission had given any report on this sorry state of affairs; 
(g)  if so, the findings of this report; and 
(h)  whether any immediate remedial measures were taken to avoid such recurrences? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD 
AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (d) No, Sir. 
This amount of diversion of Targeted Public Distrib ution System (TPDS) foodgrains was 
wrongly mentioned in Press Report in the Times of India dated 17th September, 2007. This 
Press Report seems to have used some figures of diversion reported in the study conducted 

104    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions  
by ORG MARG Report of ORG MARG study was received i n 2005. It covered data of 
2003-04 and 2004-05. This report mentioned diversion of TPDS foodgrains in a number of 
States. However, the amount mentioned in the Press Report is incorrect. It seems to have 
used economic cost of foodgrains as the basis for c alculation and seems to have assumed 
that there has been no improvement in functioning of TPDS in subsequent years. Therefore, 
this Press Report was not factually correct. 
TPDS was also evaluated by Programme Evaluation Org anisation (PEO) of Planning 
Commission. It submitted its report in 2005. This report also mentioned about diversion of 
TPDS foodgrains in many States because of exclusion  and inclusion errors in identifying 
targeted families. 
Based on PEO and ORG MARG reports, in consultation with State and Union Territory 
Governments, a 9-point Action Plan was evolved in 2 006. This Action Plan is under 
implementation in States and Union Territories since July, 2006. A copy of the 9 Point Action 
Plan is given at statement {See below) Implementation of 9 point Action Plan has le d to 
improvement in functioning of TPDS. 
(e) In addition to implementation of 9-Point Action  Plan the Government has taken a 
series of measures to strengthen TPDS. Concurrent evaluation of TPDS has been taken up in 
26 States and UTs through National Council of Appli ed Economic Research and Indian 
Institute of Public Administration. Additionally a revised Citizens Charter has been 
issued 
for adoption and implementation by State/UT Governments for facilitating use by citizens 
of provisions of Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 in relation to functioning of TPDS. 
Furthermore, to ensure that TPDS foodgrains reached the targeted families and to minimize 
scope for their diversion, APL allocations have been rationalized. Training Programmes for 
TPDS functionaries and awareness campaign for TPDS beneficiaries are being taken up. 
Computerization of TPDS has been initiateUse of new  technologies such as Global 
Positioning System is being piloted. Revised Policy on distribution of wheat flour has been 
issued. 
Statement  
9-Point Action Plan  
(i) Continuous review of the BPL and AAy lists to eliminate bogus ration cards and to 
ensure coverage of only eligible BPL and Antyodaya families. 
(ii) Ensuring leakage-free and diversion-free distribution of PDS commodities, regular 
inspection by different levels of functionaries, st rict action against guilty persons/ 
agencies. 
(iii) Involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions in  PDS operations-PRI representatives 
on Advisory Commottees, running of fair prise shops  by Panchayats and effective 
representation of Panchayati Raj representives on Vigilance Committees. 
(iv) Ensuring transparency in working of PDS displa y of BPL and AAY lists by fair 
price shops, observance of notified timings by fair price shops. 
(v) Use of Information Technology, Computerization of TPDS operations, display of 
fair price shop-wise and district wise allocations of PDS commodities on web-sites 
for public scrutiny.

(vii) Ensuring timely availability of and issuance of foodgrains by fair price shops.  
(viii) Creating awareness among public about PDS op erations, training Vigilance 
Committees of intricacies of PDS operations.

(b) Th? main reasons for low procurement in RMS 200 6-07 were less than targeted 
production, less market arrivals, negative market s entiments, high open market prices and 
high private participation. In RMS 2007-08 procurem ent of wheat was low on account of 
low market arrivals, high private participation and  the possibility that a large number of 
farmers held back stocks in expectation of higher prices in later part of the year.  
(c) Steps taken by the Government to improve procurement of wheat in RMS 2008-09

(i) The MSP for wheat has been fixed at Rs. 1000 pe r quintal for RMS 2008-09, are 
increase of Rs. 250 per quintal over the MSP fixed for RMS 2007-08, in order to

from Central Pool is also banned.

under the EC Act enabling State Government to impose stock limit on wheat.

Self Help Groups as PDS franchises  
1595. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA:  
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI:  
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION 
be pleased to state:  
 as PDS system has been grossly abused and intended beneficiaries are deprived of 
this higly subsidized mechanism, whether Government would examine to use SHGs as PDS 
franchises as is being done in Tamil Nadu; 
 if so, whether a time-bound study group will be constituted for this purpose so that it 
could in-depth examine how the 500 SHGs successfull y retail PDS commodities serving 
over 2,15,000 households in Tamil Nadu and 5600 SHGs involved in retailing kerosene in 
Orissa; and 
 whether a pilot project would be undertaken in a few select intially? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD 
AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (c) Targeted 
Public Distribution System (TPDS) is operated under joint responsibility of the Government 
of India and State/UT Governments. The Government o f India carries out procurement of 
foodgrains for the TPDS, their storage, transportat ion and allocation to the State/UT 
Governments. The responsibility for identification of eligible BPL and AAY familes within 
the respective number of BPL households estimated by the Planning Commission and issuance 
of ration cards to them, allocation of foodgrains within the State/UT and proper distribution 
of allocated TPDS foodgrains to eligible families t hrough fair price shops rests with State/ 
UT Governments.  
In consultation with State and UT Governments, it w as decided that licenses for Fair 
Price Shop (FPS) could be issued on priority to cooperatives of women and Ex-servicemen. 
Accordingly State and UT Governments have been requested to take action.  
State and UT Government have again been advised to allot FPS to Women's Self Help

 whether Government is aware that spurious and substandard drugs are being sold by drug

Government of India is aware of the problem of movement of spurious and sub-standard drugs 
in the market and has taken serious note of it. Though, being a clandestine activity it is difficult to 
assess the actual quantum of spurious/sub-standard drugs available in the market, however, a study of

under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 to make the punishment for the offenders involved in the 
manufacture or sale of spurious drugs more stringent

medicines from the suppliers which do not exceed l/6th shelf life. After due quality testing,

College & Hospital. Hence MSO neither supply any expired medicines to the Hospitals nor

1606. SHR1 S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be 
pleased to state:  
 the present life expectancy of male and female in the country; 
 whether life expectancy in the country is very less as compared to developed countries such

 if so, the details thereof and the steps proposed to be taken to increase the life expectancy in 
the country; 
 whether the infant mortality is very high in the country as compared to most of the other
